items.title: 11.1.1 Domains and Ranges of Tangent and Cotangent Functions

blocks.alt: Unit circle with centre O at the origin, axes X prime X and Y prime Y. It meets the axes at A(1, 0), B(0, 1), C(minus 1, 0) and D(0, minus 1). The terminal side OP, drawn as an arrow, makes angle theta with OX; P(x, y) is on the circle, M is the foot of the perpendicular PM on OX, OM = x and MP = y.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.1 (repeated from 11.1): unit circle with P(x, y) on the terminal side of θ (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Sine and cosine never divide by anything, so their domain is all of \(\mathbb{R}\). Tangent and cotangent are fractions:
\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}, \qquad \cot\theta = \dfrac{x}{y}\]
A fraction has no value when its denominator is \(0\). So the whole job on this page is: find the angles where the denominator becomes \(0\) and remove them from \(\mathbb{R}\).

(i) Tangent function
\[\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x},\quad x \ne 0\]
\(\Rightarrow\) terminal side \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) should not coincide with \(OY\) or \(OY'\) (the \(Y\)-axis)
\[\Rightarrow \theta \ne \pm\frac{\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{3\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{5\pi}{2}, \ldots\]
\[\Rightarrow \theta \ne (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2},\ \text{where } n \in \mathbb{Z}\]
Domain of tangent function \(= \mathbb{R} - \{x \mid x = (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2},\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the book the second line of excluded angles for the tangent (and the same line under 11.1.2) is printed jumbled: the fractions \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{5\pi}{2}\) overlap and their signs are misplaced. It should read \(\theta \ne \pm\frac{\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{3\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{5\pi}{2}, \ldots\), as written above.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does \(x = 0\) mean the \(Y\)-axis? The points with \(x = 0\) on the unit circle are \(B(0, 1)\) and \(D(0, -1)\). The terminal side reaches \(B\) at \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\frac{5\pi}{2}\), \(-\frac{3\pi}{2}\), ... and reaches \(D\) at \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\), \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\), ...
All of these are odd multiples of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\): \(1, 3, 5, \ldots\) times \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), with either sign. An odd number is \(2n + 1\), which is why the short form is \((2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\). For \(n = 0, 1, -1, -2\) it gives \(\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}, -\frac{\pi}{2}, -\frac{3\pi}{2}\).
If \(y = 1\), \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{x}\); as \(x \to 0\), \(\frac{1}{x} \to \pm\infty\), therefore the range of tangent function \(= \mathbb{R}\) = set of real numbers.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Here is the idea behind this short argument. When \(P\) moves towards \(B(0, 1)\), \(y\) gets close to \(1\) and \(x\) gets close to \(0\), so \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}\) becomes a very large number: \(\tan 89^{\circ} \approx 57.3\), \(\tan 89.9^{\circ} \approx 573\). Coming from the other side of the \(Y\)-axis, \(x\) is negative and \(\tan\theta\) becomes a very large negative number.
Another way to see it: \(\frac{y}{x}\) is the slope of the line \(OP\). As \(OP\) turns from the \(X\)-axis towards the \(Y\)-axis, its slope takes every value from \(0\) to as large as we like, and on the other side every negative value. So \(\tan\theta\) takes every real value; there is no upper or lower limit.

(ii) Cotangent function
From Figure 11.1
\[\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y},\quad y \ne 0\]
\(\Rightarrow\) terminal side \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) should not coincide with \(OX\) or \(OX'\) (the \(X\)-axis)
\[\Rightarrow \theta \ne 0, \pm\pi, \pm 2\pi, \ldots\]
\[\Rightarrow \theta \ne n\pi,\ \text{where } n \in \mathbb{Z}\]
Domain of cotangent function \(= \mathbb{R} - \{x \mid x = n\pi,\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\)
If \(x = 1\), \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{y}\); as \(y \to 0\), \(\frac{1}{y} \to \pm\infty\), therefore range of cotangent function \(= \mathbb{R}\) = set of real numbers.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
For cotangent the denominator is \(y\). The points with \(y = 0\) are \(A(1, 0)\) and \(C(-1, 0)\), reached at \(0, \pi, 2\pi, -\pi, \ldots\), i.e. at every multiple of \(\pi\): \(n\pi\).
Near these angles \(y\) is tiny and \(x\) is close to \(\pm 1\), so \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y}\) becomes as large (positive or negative) as we like. Since \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}\) wherever both exist, and \(\cot\theta = 0\) at \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\), every real number is a value of cotangent.

blocks.caption: Our summary of this page (n is any integer).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: In degrees: \(\tan\theta\) is undefined at \(90^{\circ}, 270^{\circ}, -90^{\circ}, \ldots\) and \(\cot\theta\) is undefined at \(0^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}, 360^{\circ}, \ldots\). A quick test: tangent fails where \(\cos\theta = 0\); cotangent fails where \(\sin\theta = 0\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Swapping the two lists: tangent fails on the \(Y\)-axis (\(x = 0\)), cotangent on the \(X\)-axis (\(y = 0\)).
2. Forgetting \(\theta = 0\) for cotangent: \(n = 0\) gives \(0\pi = 0\), and \(\cot 0\) is undefined.
3. Writing the range of tangent as \([-1, 1]\) like sine. Tangent is not bounded.
